role.text: In view because this Story happens here.
Ships from China came each spring, thirty or forty in a usual year by Morga's account.

The marker shows present-day Manila; it is not a surveyed position for the city of 1602.

placeContext.headerLine: A county seat in Fujian, Ming China

role.text: In view because a historian names it as the home port of the ships in this Story.
A historian calls it the principal home port of the Chinese merchant fleets.
In 1589 the Ming court fixed the number of ship licences and gave 16 to Luzon.
Its customs officers reported that ships came back from Luzon carrying only silver coins.
The marker shows the present-day town of Haicheng. Where the ships of 1602 lay is not located.

role.text: In view because the goods of this Story were sold here.
Morga wrote that cargoes were taken to the Parián or to other warehouses outside the city, and sold there freely.
In 1603 the governor wrote of it as standing on the front between the river and the sea.
Historians put the Chinese of Manila at many thousands by 1600 and disagree on the number.

connection.directionNote: Fujian to Manila and back, across the South China Sea. Goods one way, silver the other. Directional; not symmetric.
connection.directionFigureText: Merchants from Fujian  →  enabled  →  the trade at Manila, for silver

spatial.originText: Haicheng (Yuegang), Fujian · settlement precision · named as the home port by a historian; Morga names the provinces only
spatial.routeStatement: Ships from Fujian came to Manila each spring with silk and other goods, and went home with silver coin. The Ming court licensed the voyage: in 1589 it fixed the number of ship licences, and sixteen were for Luzon. Morga, writing in 1609, says thirty or forty ships usually came each year; the customs count for 1602 has eighteen. After the massacre of 1603 the ships came again in 1604. No Source we have read names a ship, a merchant or a cargo for 1602.
spatial.accountsSentence: After the massacre of 1603 the ships came again in 1604.

connection.scholarlyStanding: Von Glahn (1996) and Iaccarino (2011) both describe this trade as silk for silver and place its height around 1600. They disagree on whether America or Japan was China's larger source of silver at the time.

mechanismText.text: Merchants in Fujian had silk and other goods that sold at Manila.
The Spaniards at Manila had silver coin from New Spain, and the Chinese traders took payment in nothing else.
The Ming court allowed the voyage under licence from 1589.
So the ships came each spring and went home with silver.
Historians explain the pull by what silver was worth in China.
How much silver went this way in 1602 is not known. The figures run from one million pesos a year to five.
This is how merchants from Fujian came to supply Manila for silver. The Claims it rests on are listed beneath it. Most of them are Spanish voices.

participants.text: Merchants of Fujian, who owned the goods and came with them or sent agents
The Ming court, which licensed ships for Luzon from 1589
Customs officers at Haicheng, who reported ships returning with only silver coins
The governor of Fujian, Xu Xueju, who wrote in 1604 why his people went
Spanish officers at Manila, who valued each cargo and took three per cent
Spaniards at Manila, who bought the goods with silver and reals
Chinese residents of Manila, in whose quarter the goods were sold
Merchants of Mexico and of Peru, whose money came over beyond the limit

connection.evidenceIndependenceNote: Two Spanish writers at Manila, Morga and Fernández de Castro. On the Chinese side, the court record of 1589 and one governor of 1604 in a historian's translation. The ship count is one series, from Chaunu.

reverseDisclosure.body: Silver into Fujian is the other half of this trade, and it is in this Connection's Claims. What that silver did at the ships' home port is a different Connection, with its own mechanism and its own Sources; it is in the Story "The ships that came home with coin". What the silver did in the rest of China is not researched.

connection.reverseRelationshipNote: A separate Connection, not an inversion of this one. Silver's effect in China is not created in this fixture.

additionalConnections.leadIn: A second Connection leads to Manila: silver from Peru, about 1590 to 1604.
additionalConnections.directionNote: From Peru by sea to Acapulco, then west to Manila. Silver one way, Chinese goods the other. Directional; not symmetric.
additionalConnections.directionFigureText: Silver from Peru  →  contributed to  →  the silver spent at Manila

spatial.originText: Potosí · settlement precision · the letters of the time say Peru; that Potosí silver was in it is one historian's reading, Kris Lane's
spatial.targetText: Manila · settlement precision · by way of Acapulco
spatial.routeStatement: In the 1590s merchants from Peru took silver by sea to Acapulco and bought the Chinese goods landed there by the ships from Manila. The viceroy of Peru reported that a dozen ships sailed for Mexico in 1593 and early 1594 and left Peru bare of silver. Two or three million pesos a year went out this way, historians write, and most of it was sent on to the Philippines. In June 1582 the crown forbade ships to sail between Peru and the Philippines, and the sale of Philippine goods in Peru. The limits on ships between Peru and New Spain came later, from 1604. Before that, one ship from the Philippines is known to have reached Peru, in 1582, with goods. No Source of the time that we have read names Potosí silver on a ship. One historian, Kris Lane, writes that it was there, and that how much is uncertain. No Source we have read says how the silver came down from Potosí to the coast.

additionalConnections.scholarlyStanding: Woodrow Borah (1954), Guillermina del Valle Pavón (2005) and Kris Lane (2019) all describe silver from Peru going to Acapulco for Chinese goods and on to Manila. That Potosí silver was on the ships is Lane's reading alone. Borah and del Valle Pavón name Potosí as the mine behind Peru's wealth and as a market for the goods. Del Valle Pavón cites Borah, so these are not two separate readings. Lane writes that how much Potosí silver reached Asia this way remains uncertain.

mechanismText.text: Peru had silver and was short of goods. Two historians name Potosí as its great mine and as a market for the goods.
Chinese goods landed at Acapulco cost far less than goods from Spain, and Potosí's shops sold Chinese silk.
So merchants from Peru came to New Spain with silver, as the king himself wrote in 1603.
The viceroy of Peru reported a dozen ships for Mexico in 1593 and early 1594.
Most of the silver, historians write, was sent on to the Philippines.
At Manila, Morga and a lawyer of about 1602 both name money from Peru.
In June 1582 the crown forbade sailing between Peru and the Philippines and the sale of Philippine goods in Peru. From 1604 it also cut back the ships between Peru and New Spain.
Earlier, the governor of the Philippines sent ships for Peru in 1580 and 1581. One is known to have arrived, in 1582, with goods.
Kris Lane (2019) writes that Potosí silver went on these ships, and that how much reached Asia is uncertain. That is his reading. No letter of the time that we have read says Potosí.
This is how silver from Peru came to be spent at Manila. The Claims it rests on are listed beneath it. The letters of the time say Peru; that some of it was Potosí's is Lane's reading.

participants.text: Merchants of Peru, who came to Acapulco with silver
The viceroy of Peru, who reported the ships and the loss of silver
Merchants of Mexico and Peru with agents at Manila
The king, who forbade the sailing in 1582 and cut back the ships from 1604

additionalConnections.evidenceIndependenceNote: No eyewitness of the whole route. The viceroy of Peru's report reaches us through two historians, and the second cites the first. The king repeats his viceroys' letters. Morga and Fernández de Castro wrote at Manila and say "Peru", not Potosí. Lane names Potosí; we have not read the notes he rests on. No Andean Source, no merchant's account book and no ship's register is among them. The miners and mill workers of Potosí are in none of them.

reverseDisclosure.body: Chinese goods went the other way, from Acapulco to Peru and up to Potosí's shops. That leg has a Claim here but is a different Connection, not researched.

additionalConnections.reverseRelationshipNote: A separate Connection, not an inversion of this one.

readingPaneEmpty.heading: One moment, and how we know it.
body: Select the Event on the map, or in the list beneath it, to open its Story.

This Moment is Manila in 1602: the ships that came from China each spring, and the one Connection this pilot explains for it, merchants from Fujian and the trade at Manila, silk for silver. Haicheng, in Fujian, is drawn at the wider view as the home port a historian names. The Story goes on to 1603, when very many of the Chinese of Manila were killed.

segments.text: We don't know why Morga's thirty or forty ships a year and the customs count of eighteen for 1602 differ.
It may be a poor year, ships that paid no duty, or a round number. No Source we have read says.
We don't know how much silver left Manila for China in 1602. One million pesos a year was counted, three or four million is one historian's estimate, and five million was claimed at the time.
No Source of the time that we have read names Potosí silver on a ship at Acapulco. They say Peru. One historian, Kris Lane, writes that Potosí silver was there, and that how much is uncertain.
We have no Philippine voice for this year, and no words of a Chinese resident of Manila. No Source we have read for the silver from Peru has the words of anyone who mined or milled it.
We don't know how many people were killed: every figure we have read belongs to someone, and they differ.
We don't know why it began: each side gives its own account, and the historian who compared them writes that the reasons remain unclear.
We have no words from a Chinese resident of Manila who lived through it.
We have no account from the Philippine troops who fought beside the Spaniards.
